blocks.cap: Rei's room in the dead hour of the night

blocks.p: At 3:11 the phone lit the ceiling white. The buzz against the pillow went through his skull like a dentist's drill.

It was the dead hour, the hour when even Tokyo turns its lights down. The trains had stopped. The last taxis had gone home. Outside, the only sound was an air conditioner unit humming on the next balcony. Rei had fallen asleep in his clothes. He came up out of a dream about water and had the phone in his hand before he knew he was awake.
There was no greeting. There was no small name, and no warmth aimed anywhere.
dont come to kita dont come here its not him answering rei i can feel it making the wall thin go to itsuki burn the

It stopped there. There was no full stop. The sentence was cut off the way the journal entry for the fourteenth of August was cut off, in the middle, like a hand pulled off a page. And the typing mistakes were wrong in the right way. They were Gin's mistakes. Gin had never learned to type cleanly with his thumbs, and his letters always stumbled to the left. He had not waited for the phone to correct him. The missing capital letters were pure panic.
Rei had spent the whole night learning that the smooth voice was the enemy. And here was the broken voice. His heart went through the floor toward it, like a stone dropped down a well.
He sat up in the dark with the phone too bright in his hand and read the message nine times.

Rei lived in Kita. But he knew Gin did not mean the flat. He meant the deep part of the ward, the canal and the thin spot, the place where the wall was weakest. Everything in Rei that was a brother wanted to be out of the door and down there now. And that was the one thing the message begged him not to do.

Then a colder thought came. The thing wearing Gin wanted him away from Kita. So a voice telling him to stay away might be the thing too. Except that the broken voice had said something the thing would never say. It had named the thinning of the wall. It had confessed the plan. It had pointed him at Itsuki, and at burning something. A gatekeeper does not hand out the address of its own gate.

Unless. Unless this was the most patient trap of all. A trap that let the trapped man come up for exactly one message. Because a brother who is forbidden to come will run to the forbidden place faster than any brother who is only invited.
He could feel the exact shape of the hope and the exact shape of the hook. They sat in the same place. He could not pull them apart just by wanting to.

He reached for the Archive on the floor beside the mattress, where he had left it at dawn. He did not need to search. He knew the page now. It was in the chapter on demons, at the end of the list of signs, in a box Gin had marked urgent.

doc.title: Gin's book. Chapter Nine. Urgent comment.
lines: The secondary signal in partial possession. I want to state this as clearly as the documentation allows. The host is still there.

The four seconds where the host surfaces are the most important four seconds of the encounter. They confirm the host is present. They may carry information. They are almost certainly the only communication the host can manage.
Do not miss them by only reading the dominant signal. Look for the secondary.

blocks.p: A few seconds of thumbs. That was all a man could manage from inside, when the thing driving him looked away. And Gin had used his few seconds to type a warning, a place, a friend's name and half of an instruction.
Rei turned back a few pages, to a part he had skimmed the first time. He had skimmed it because he had not wanted it to be about anyone he knew.

blocks.cap: Partial possession, the host still in the chair

doc.title: Gin's book. Chapter Six. Possession. The Two States.
lines: Partial possession. The demon occupies and drives the host body while the host soul remains inside. The host is conscious, aware, experiencing everything done through their body, but cannot surface except under specific conditions and cannot control their own actions. The demon uses the host's memories and relationships as cover. The host is trapped, not gone.
This state is unstable. It progresses over time toward full possession as the demon's hold deepens and the host's resistance wears down.

Full possession, or soul ejection. The demon completes the fusion and forces the host soul out entirely, into the Threshold. The soul has witnessed the whole of the partial possession, and in that state it turns heavily toward the Demon or Suffering Being paths. The body goes on under complete demon control. The host is gone.
After ejection the demon can still be removed from the body, but the host must then be found and guided in the Threshold before their path sets. That is a different and much harder operation.
Exorcism during partial possession is the recovery with the best outcome. The host returns changed. They carry the memory of the whole duration. They do not return undamaged. They return.

blocks.p: Rei read the page slowly, and he put it into plain words for himself. There were two kinds of possession. In the first, the demon drove the body like a car, but the owner was still inside, in the passenger seat, awake and seeing everything. In the second, the demon threw the owner out of the car altogether, into the Threshold, the crowded layer just behind the veil where the newly dead wander. From there the owner might never find the way back.

They return. Rei read those two words until they stopped being words. Gin was in the first state. He had to be. A man who had been thrown out could not have reached for a phone. But Gin's own page said the first state did not stay the first state. It got deeper. Every message the smooth voice sent was a little more of the hold settling into place. And every time Gin managed to come up, it cost him something he might not get back.

The seasickness was back, his own floor tilting. For once he was grateful for it, because it meant he was still reading and had not yet decided. He checked himself the way the Running Low page told him to. Did he feel reachable, as if a door were open somewhere? No. Only tired, and frightened, and hungry. So he made himself get up. He ate a cold rice ball from the fridge, standing at the counter in the dark, and drank a glass of water. Gin would have said that before anything else. Eat. Sleep. He could not sleep. He could eat.

Out of the window, the last Obon lanterns along the canal had burned down and gone out. The dead, he supposed, had been guided home. The living were left holding their phones. He did not text back yet. He made himself be a person who could wait sixty seconds. He watched the screen, waiting for the smooth voice to come and clean up after the broken one.
At 3:16 the smooth voice arrived. Its speed told him more than any sentence could.
I'm sorry... I don't even know what I wrote, I think I fell asleep texting, I've been so tired. Ignore that, please. I'm fine. Don't go anywhere on account of a half-asleep message.

It was reasonable. In its way it was even true. A tired man, confused, not himself. But it was fast. It was fast in a way the earlier replies had never been fast. It was fast like something that had been caught and was now hurrying. And the warmth in it was pointed harder than usual. There was more please in it. More aim.

The broken text had said burn and Itsuki and the wall. The smooth text wanted him to put all three down to a sleepy man typing, and to go back to bed. Tonight he had learned whose interest each of those served.

He held the two messages side by side, five minutes apart, and he understood what he had just seen. He had watched the seam happen live. It was not in a journal found afterwards. It was not in handwriting studied in the cold light. It had happened in front of him, in real time. The old voice had come up for a few broken seconds, and the new one had rushed in to plaster over the hole.

The thing had not denied the plan. It could not deny it fast enough, because Gin had already said it out loud. So it did the next thing, the thing it was best at. It turned the confession into a symptom. It offered Rei the comfort of not believing his own brother. That was the whole trick, he saw now. It did not fight his love for Gin. It recruited it. It asked his love to please be reasonable, and to please not make a tired man feel watched.
He put the phone face-down on the floor, where he could not see the next message arrive. He breathed. He let the certainty build itself slowly, so that it would be certainty and not just hope.

Gin was in there. He had come up. It had cost him something to come up, and it had cost the thing something to push him down again. The pushing had been fast and frightened, and frightened was information. Whatever Rei did at dawn, he would do it knowing his brother was alive enough to break a window for a few seconds. And he would do it knowing that the thing holding him was, for the first time all night, working faster than it would like.
The lanterns were out. It was the hour when the city forgets itself. Rei had somewhere to be when it remembered.
